items.stem: State, in terms of electrons, what reduction is.
items.modelAnswer: Reduction is electron gain (oxidation is electron loss).

items.stem: State what ions reaching an electrode form after losing or gaining electrons.
items.modelAnswer: They form neutral substances, which are discharged as the products.

items.stem: Explain why the charges on the two sides of a half equation must balance.
items.modelAnswer: Because electrons carry charge: the electrons lost or gained at the electrode set the charge moved, so a correct half equation shows the same total charge on both sides.

items.stem: During electrolysis, a negatively charged chloride ion reaches the anode. State whether the chloride ion is oxidised or reduced, and what it does with electrons.
items.modelAnswer: It is oxidised — negative ions lose electrons at the anode, so the chloride ion loses an electron.

items.stem: State the substance formed at the cathode during the electrolysis of molten lead(II) bromide.
items.modelAnswer: Molten lead metal, from the half equation Pb2+ + 2e- → Pb.

items.stem: State the product formed at the anode when a molten chloride salt is electrolysed.
items.modelAnswer: Chlorine gas — the same form writes chloride discharge: 2Cl- → Cl2 + 2e-, oxidation.

items.stem: Explain why the bromide half equation 2Br- → Br2 + 2e- is classified as oxidation.
items.modelAnswer: Because the bromide ions lose electrons — 2Br- → Br2 + 2e- — and oxidation is defined as electron loss.

items.stem: Molten potassium bromide is electrolysed. State the product at the cathode, and whether its half equation is oxidation or reduction.
items.modelAnswer: Potassium metal forms at the cathode: K+ + e- → K is reduction (electron gain).

items.stem: State the gas produced at the cathode during the electrolysis of dilute sulfuric acid.
items.modelAnswer: Hydrogen gas — the cathode half equation is 2H+ + 2e- → H2.

items.stem: State the product formed at the cathode when aqueous copper(II) sulfate is electrolysed, and name the ion it comes from.
items.modelAnswer: Copper metal, from the Cu2+ ions: Cu2+ + 2e- → Cu.

items.stem: Explain why the hydroxide ion, rather than water, appears in the oxidation half equation for alkaline solutions.
items.modelAnswer: Because alkaline solutions contain OH- ions — the hydroxide is present to be discharged, so it appears in the oxidation half equation instead of water.

items.stem: A student electrolyses dilute sulfuric acid and collects the gas bubbling off at the anode. State the gas collected.
items.modelAnswer: Oxygen — water is oxidised at the anode: 2H2O → O2 + 4H+ + 4e-.

items.stem: State the two starting substances used to make the copper(II) sulfate in this practical.
items.modelAnswer: Copper(II) oxide (the base) and dilute sulfuric acid.

items.stem: State how the copper(II) oxide is added to the hot acid.
items.modelAnswer: Slowly, with stirring, until it is in excess.

items.stem: Explain why the excess solid must be removed before the solution is crystallised.
items.modelAnswer: Because filtering removes the excess solid base, leaving only the salt solution in the evaporating basin — the aim is a pure, dry batch of crystals, so leftover base must not contaminate it.

items.stem: A student forgets to warm the dilute sulfuric acid before adding the copper(II) oxide. State the effect this has on the reaction with the base.
items.modelAnswer: The reaction is slower — warming the dilute sulfuric acid gently speeds up the reaction with the base, so cold acid reacts more slowly.

items.stem: State the purpose of heating the solution gently at the start of the evaporation stage.
items.modelAnswer: To evaporate water and make the solution saturated.

items.stem: State how the crystals are separated from the leftover solution after crystallisation.
items.modelAnswer: The excess solution is decanted away, and the crystals are allowed to dry.

items.stem: Explain why the filtrate is left in a warm place to dry.
items.modelAnswer: So the solution can dry out and the dissolved copper(II) sulfate can crystallise — leaving it warm lets good crystals form as the water leaves.

items.stem: A student dips a cold glass rod into the evaporating basin and no crystals form on its end. State what this shows about the solution, and what should be done next.
items.modelAnswer: The solution is not saturated yet — keep heating gently to evaporate more water until crystals do form on a cold rod.

items.stem: State the family name of the metals found in the first column of the periodic table.
items.modelAnswer: The alkali metals — lithium, sodium, potassium, rubidium, caesium and francium.

items.stem: State the two products formed when any Group 1 metal reacts with water.
items.modelAnswer: A metal hydroxide and hydrogen gas.

items.stem: Explain why all the alkali metals share the same characteristic chemical behaviour.
items.modelAnswer: Because each of them carries a single electron in its outermost shell, so they react in the same characteristic ways.

items.stem: A student finds a metal that can be cut easily with a knife. State the family it likely belongs to, and one other physical property it should show.
items.modelAnswer: An alkali metal — they are soft and easily cut, with low densities and low melting points.

items.stem: State how lithium's and sodium's reactions with water differ.
items.modelAnswer: Lithium fizzes gently on the water surface, while sodium races about — the reaction grows more vigorous down the group.

items.stem: State what forms on the surface of an alkali metal left exposed to air.
items.modelAnswer: A dull oxide coating — oxygen draws the coating across the shiny surface.

items.stem: Explain why melting points fall on descending Group 1.
items.modelAnswer: Because the attractive forces between the outer electrons and the positive ions weaken down the group, so less energy is needed to melt the metal.

items.stem: Francium sits at the bottom of Group 1. State whether francium should tarnish in air faster or slower than potassium does.
items.modelAnswer: Faster — tarnishing speeds up down the group, mirroring the water-reaction trend.

items.stem: State which Group 1 metal is the most reactive, and where it sits in the group.
items.modelAnswer: Francium, at the bottom of the group (lithium, at the top, is the least reactive).

items.stem: State which Group 1 metals should out-react lithium, sodium and potassium with both air and water.
items.modelAnswer: Rubidium, caesium and francium.

items.stem: Explain why francium is predicted to be the most reactive alkali metal.
items.modelAnswer: Because the metals grow more reactive with both air and water on descending the group, and francium sits at the very bottom.

items.stem: Caesium sits below rubidium in Group 1. Predict whether caesium's melting point is lower or higher than rubidium's.
items.modelAnswer: Lower — melting points fall on descending the group, and caesium sits below rubidium.
